A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ISAC and IntraCompBench. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–G support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting and relocation.

before.justification: v2 reports original generation experiments, baseline comparisons, ablations and seed-stability measurements, including Tables 2–6 and the appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and reports additional model comparisons, evaluator validation, preference scores and sensitivity analyses.

M1.justification: Foreground gating, self-attention clustering, MPO losses, semantic binding and the linear loss schedule are retained. Both latent optimization and latent selection already appear in v2; moving Algorithm 2 into the main text and introducing the ISACLO label do not change the method. Expanded parser details do not establish a procedural revision.

E1.justification: Both versions use HRS-Bench, T2I-CompBench including Numeracy, and IntraCompBench with the same 37 COCO classes and 2–5-instance tasks. Text-to-image and layout-to-image coverage remain. Added backbones, evaluators and internal-control perturbations do not introduce new datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated comparisons with DOS in Table 2, CO3 and DeLeaker in Table 11, and GPT-Image-1.5 and Nano Banana 2 in Table 13. Conversely, A&E is removed from the image-quality comparison corresponding to v2 Table 13 and v3 Table 15, although it remains elsewhere.

E3.justification: Added evaluation settings include Flux.2-dev latent selection, 8-step Z-Image-Turbo and 4-step Flux.2-klein-4B generation, GPT-5.5 evaluation, and PickScore/HPSv3 metrics. New controlled experiments perturb internal counts and clustering frequency. These extend the evaluation design; the original benchmark sampling and retained experiments' stated settings largely remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds foreground-threshold sensitivity, quantitative coordinate ablation, internal-count mismatch tests, clustering-frequency trade-offs and detector-independent validation. The existing loss comparison gains Dice and top-5%/top-10% MPO variants. Commercial-model failure examples and preference analysis also extend the supplementary evidence; earlier schedule, clustering-algorithm, seed and layer analyses remain.

E5.justification: v3 Table 14 introduces statistical agreement analysis through Pearson correlations between detector and GPT-5.5 evaluations, reporting 0.73 and 0.75. The existing 30-seed Numeracy means and standard deviations, and 10-seed IntraCompBench practice, remain unchanged; no additional confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: Substantial new results cover modern comparators, few-step models, preference scores and sensitivity tests. For example, v3 Table 5 newly reports Flux.2-dev class/instance averages of 88%/87% without ISAC and 92%/92% with latent selection. Retained accuracy results mostly match. Table 2 changes TEBOpt's SD3.5-M costs from 139 s/74.5 GB to 42 s/28.8 GB, while Appendix Table 19 retains the older values. Table 4's percentage-to-fraction conversion is only equivalent rounding.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix C.6 newly defines top-k% MPO alternatives by averaging the largest overlap products, extending the loss definitions used in ablations. The principal attention, masking and loss equations remain equivalent after renumbering; no new theorem, proof or derivation is added.

C1.justification: The central ISAC and IntraCompBench contributions remain. The abstract, introduction and conclusion now emphasize improving open-weight models and narrowing their gap with commercial systems. The abstract also qualifies v2's claim of requiring no external models to requiring no external vision models.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations of count-mismatch failures, the value of frequent reclustering, and difficulties with small or thin foreground objects. It interprets new commercial-model and VLM results as evidence about applicability and detector bias. Appendix C.3 replaces the earlier A&E-based quality discussion with stronger claims about preference and absence of quality trade-offs; the existing 3D/transparency limitation remains.

D1.justification: v3 reports code and IntraCompBench availability through a project link, replacing v2's future code-release promise. Appendix A.1 newly specifies omitting global or ambiguously assigned attribute-binding pairs, and Figure 2 documents averaging masks over denoising timesteps. These are access and implementation disclosures, not demonstrated changes to existing experiments.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands substantially around open-weight versus commercial systems and contemporary methods including DOS, CO3 and DeLeaker. Related work more explicitly distinguishes CLIP-dependent embedding methods and token-conditioned structural grouping from ISAC. v2's categorical claim of being the first training-free method for instance-level control in Section 2 is removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related-work discussion and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. Latent selection moves from Appendix C.1 into Section 4.3, the loss-metric discussion moves into the appendix, Appendix C is reorganized, and references move before the appendices. Terminology, title and author information also change.

P2.justification: v3 substantially redesigns page layout, typography and figure/table placement, including paired Tables 3–4 and Figures 6–7. It adds threshold, commercial-performance, commercial-failure and clustering-frequency figures, plus new comparison tables and preference columns. Some displays are reused: Figure 7 draws examples from v2's appendix, and latent-selection displays move into the main text.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens an already extensive empirical study with useful count-sensitivity tests, VLM cross-checks and contemporary comparisons, improving support for applicability and robustness. The gain is moderated by removing A&E from the quality comparison, treating automated preference scores as stronger evidence of preserved visual quality than they establish, and leaving revised TEBOpt costs unexplained against retained appendix values. Overall, the added validation provides a positive but limited net improvement.
